knowledge.statement: A leader whose main loop is stalled past its lease can return VerifyLeader success while a successor already leads the cluster at a higher term, and a caller acting on that success reads state the cluster has moved past. Two executions of the endpoint probe show the overlap in twelve of twelve trials with eight successes (three of six, then five of six); a third execution reads the FSM directly and finds the stalled leader still holding the value committed before the partition while the successor holds the value committed after it, in all five trials, with the verify returning success in two of them (parsed indices 1 and 7) and leadership loss in the other three.
knowledge.conditions: Three voters plus one non-voter; the leader isolated from both other voters and from the non-voter while the request is registered; the leader's main loop then blocked inside StoreLogs for 900ms by a client Apply; the non-voter reconnected 250-500ms later; HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms, in-memory transports in one process, mock FSM recording applied commands.
knowledge.changed_premise: The premise is unchanged and the consequence is now measured rather than inferred: the earlier executions established the overlap and the endpoint, and this one reads the state machine on both nodes so the stale read is shown directly. The success rate across executions is recorded as it was rather than averaged into a single figure.

interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM. The question was whether its success establishes voter-majority contact; the execution says it does not. In the retained run of the three-partition probe, the leader whose only reachable peer was the non-voter returned success in 0ms while its own latest configuration reported three voters, one non-voter and a quorum size of 2, and the leader was still in Leader state (parsed event index 1); the control partition that kept one voter reachable also returned success, which shows the harness does observe a genuine acknowledgement path (index 3); the control partition with no reachable peer did not return success at all, returning 'leadership lost while committing log' after 202ms with the node in Follower state, so the leader cannot reach the threshold on its own vote and the non-voter acknowledgement is what satisfied it in the first case (index 5). All three declared comparisons hold with the setup event matched as admission (correlations 1->0, 3->2, 5->4). The source explains the mechanism: verifyLeader asks every entry of leaderState.replState to acknowledge, startStopReplication creates such an entry for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, any successful AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot reply from such a peer calls notifyAll(true) and increments verifyFuture.votes, and the threshold compared against is quorumSize(), counted over voters alone. The same package treats voter eligibility strictly in its other leadership tests: checkLeaderLease does not count a non-voter, requestVote refuses a candidate that holds no vote, and quorumSize itself counts only voters, so the verify path is the outlier rather than a deliberate relaxation. The consequence for reads stays bounded and is not what this receipt measures. The leader's lease is voter-only, and both Config.Validate and ReloadConfig enforce LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, so the old leader is normally removed before a voter majority elects a successor; the no-peer control is exactly that lease firing at 202ms with a 200ms lease. What the receipt does establish is the weaker but unconditional part: for an interval in which the leader exchanged nothing with any other voter, VerifyLeader reports success, so a caller relying on that call for read consistency is really relying on the lease timer rather than on the acknowledgements VerifyLeader collected. The same file shows the omission is not a considered relaxation of voter eligibility: electSelf and preElectSelf build the very same voter-sized threshold, and both iterate the leader's latest configuration asking only servers whose Suffrage is Voter, so a candidate neither solicits nor counts a non-voter's grant even though nothing on the granting side stops a non-voter from granting a vote if it were asked. Only the verify path asks every replication peer. That contrast is recorded as its own Behaviour so the finding is not reused without it, and it turns the question's answer from 'the success signal is weaker than its documentation' into 'the success signal contradicts the eligibility rule the same decisions use everywhere else'. The consequence that this account previously kept conditional is now witnessed. A separate probe registers the verify request while the leader is isolated from every peer, stalls the leader's main loop inside StoreLogs for 900ms so its lease case cannot run, and reconnects only the non-voter once a voter majority has had time to elect. In all six trials a different server was sampled in Leader state at term 3 before the verdict (first at 319-454ms) while the old leader stayed at term 2, and in three of them (result events at parsed indices 3, 7 and 9) the old leader's VerifyLeader returned success at 931ms - the moment the stall released the loop, by which time the non-voter's acknowledgement had already been counted on a replication goroutine. The other three trials answered 'leadership lost while committing log', so the outcome is a per-trial choice between the two ready cases, but the successful ones are exactly the stale-read verdict the API says it prevents: a caller told 'still leader' while a successor already led at a higher term. Two details keep this from contradicting the earlier refuted child question, which asked whether a request *queued during* the stall can succeed: it cannot, because the main loop must be running to register the request, and that is why the successful construction registers first and stalls afterwards. The parent defect claim is unchanged; what changes is its consequence, which is no longer conditional on an unobserved interleaving but demonstrated under a stated condition. The repeat of that probe strengthens the witness rather than merely confirming it: in the second run (receipt 2f645950e0334342b1f7392ed1c1f286, result events at parsed indices 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11) the successor overlap again appeared in all six trials, with a different server first sampled in Leader state at term 3 between 345ms and 511ms while the old leader stayed at term 2, and five of the six trials returned VerifyLeader success at 931-932ms - only the 250ms reconnection answered 'leadership lost while committing log'. Across the two runs the overlap holds in twelve of twelve trials and success in eight of twelve, so what reproduces is the overlap, while the verdict itself remains a per-trial choice between the ready verify case and the ready lease case. The account, its defect claim and its resolved gap answer are otherwise unchanged. The last limitation this account carried is now closed by a probe that reads the FSM instead of inferring the consequence. Each trial commits the value 'old' through the leader and waits for it to reach every node, partitions the leader, stalls its main loop, lets a successor at term 3 commit the value 'new', reconnects only the non-voter, and then reads the mock FSM on both nodes after the verify returns. All five trials show the divergence the consequence needs: the stalled leader's FSM still held 'old' while the successor held 'new' (comparisons at parsed indices 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9, the latter two confirming the successor's value), and in the two trials where the verify returned success (indices 1 and 7, reconnections 300ms and 450ms) a caller following the documented pattern would have read 'old' from a node it had just been told was still the leader, while the cluster's state was 'new'. The other three trials answered 'leadership lost while committing log', so the read only matters when the verify succeeds; the verdict remains the per-trial choice recorded earlier.

d704b04e706144dc964ff451359eda19-gap-0.explanation: Resolved. The legal condition is a leader whose main loop is stalled past its lease while a non-voter it can reach becomes reachable during the stall: configuration routes are not needed. The new probe registered a VerifyLeader request while the leader was isolated from every peer, blocked its main loop inside StoreLogs for 900ms so the lease case could not fire, and reconnected only the non-voter after 250-500ms. In all six trials a successor was sampled in Leader state at term 3 before the verdict (first at 319-454ms) with the old leader still at term 2; in three trials the verify returned success at 931ms, when the stall released the loop and the already-counted non-voter vote was delivered, and the other three answered leadership loss. The earlier bound still explains normal operation: without a stall the lease case is always ready by the time a successor can exist, so the two cannot overlap; the stall is what removes that protection, because the lease check runs on the main loop.

knowledge.assertion: The FSM read at the stalled leader still holds the pre-partition value while the successor holds the new one, so a caller that acts on a successful verify reads state the cluster has moved past.

counterevidence: The leadership lease still bounds the ordinary case: without a stalled main loop the lease case is served no later than LeaderLeaseTimeout, which is why the six-trial probe needed a 900ms store stall to reach the condition.

The witness depends on a non-voter in the configuration and reachable from the stalled leader; the earlier controls show that without any acknowledgement the same call fails (no-peer control) and that a voter acknowledgement is the legitimate path.
The stalled leader never adopted the successor's term (leader_term_after stayed 2 in every trial), which is what makes the two leaders coexist and the verdict stale.

The split between success and leadership loss varies between executions of the same probe: the first run returned success in three of six trials and leadership loss in the other three, while the repeat returned success in five of six (only the 250ms reconnection answered leadership loss). Across both runs eight of twelve trials returned success, and the successor overlap held in all twelve, so the overlap is what reproduces while the verdict remains a per-trial choice.
limitations: The end-to-end read is demonstrated in two of five trials of the latest probe: the stale read needs the verify to return success, and the other three trials answered leadership loss, in which case a correct caller would not go on to read the FSM at all.

The witness rests on two executions of the same fixed probe (receipts 01617c5662f34c3eb21857602f6cac4f and 2f645950e0334342b1f7392ed1c1f286), twelve trials in total, of which eight returned success; the probe is not repeated under different timeouts or stall lengths.

The verdict arrives when the stall releases the main loop (931-932ms in every trial), so the success is returned at the first loop iteration after the acknowledgement had already been counted, not while the loop was blocked.
In-memory transports in one process with 200ms timeouts and a 900ms stall; multi-host clocks and process suspensions are not covered.

The stall is a wrapper around the log store that blocks StoreLogs on the leader's main thread, and the non-voter is reconnected by transport calls; both are supplied conditions rather than faults observed in a deployment.
interpretations.joint_history: Two harnesses contribute to this account. The three-partition probe of experiment d704b04e706144dc964ff451359eda19-experiment (receipts b02d5ff23a504a8ea38116085ba8e23c and 107a6d6c816d448da2b7ff6e3145bac1) establishes that VerifyLeader succeeds with only a non-voter's acknowledgement and fails with none, using the same four-server build, the same 200ms timeouts and the same in-memory transports. Experiment 29a71a7377a44fdbac949d4808f7b847-experiment (receipt 01617c5662f34c3eb21857602f6cac4f) reuses that build and adds the stall, the isolated registration and the late non-voter reconnection. The two are compatible because the topology, configuration and suffrage of every server are identical; the later one supplies the additional condition rather than changing a shared premise. The repeat re-executed experiment 29a71a7377a44fdbac949d4808f7b847-experiment unchanged in a clean copy, so its receipt shares the harness, the timeouts, the reconnection delays and the measurement fields with the first. A third revision, 6dde68d44bab41fda8cd5280bf6f72ac-experiment, reuses that harness and adds committed values plus reads of the mock FSM on both nodes, so its values are comparable with the earlier runs' endpoints and terms.
